## Abstract

Background: Cognitive interventions that incorporate compensatory strategies may be

particularly effective for individuals with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI).  This meta-analysis

evaluated the efficacy of compensatory cognitive interventions for individuals with MCI.

Specifically, the following were evaluated: (1) the overall efficacy across cognitive outcomes, (2)

effectiveness on different cognitive domains, and (3) influence of study-level moderators.

Method: Database searches were conducted, and relevant studies were screened for inclusion

criteria and underwent data extraction. A meta-analysis was performed across 23 included

studies, followed by subgroup moderator and sensitivity analyses.

Results: The overall pooled effect size across all cognitive outcomes was g = 0.37, though

sensitivity analyses adjusting for small-study bias suggested an effect in the small range (g =

0.22). Domain-specific analyses indicated significant positive effects on mental status and

general cognition (g = 0.31), memory (g = 0.43), working memory and attention (g = 0.44),

executive functioning (g = 0.28), and language (g = 0.29). Subgroup analyses revealed no overall

significant differences between intervention approach, strategy type, control type, or intervention

format. However, multicomponent approaches yielded significant effects for executive

functioning and working memory, external strategies showed larger effects for memory and

working memory/attention, and group-based formats provided greater improvements across

outcomes.

Conclusion: Compensatory-based interventions offer small-to-moderate benefits for individuals

with MCI, particularly in the domains of memory and attention/working memory. While study-

level moderators did not demonstrate significant differences, trends suggest that multicomponent

approaches, using both external and internal strategies, and a group intervention format may

confer some benefits.

## Background

Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) represents a transitional stage between age-related

cognitive decline and dementia (Petersen et al., 2001). The most widely used diagnostic criteria

for MCI include: 1) subjective cognitive complaints, 2) objective impairment in one or more

cognitive domains, 3) preserved independence in everyday functioning, and 4) does not meet the

criteria for dementia (Albert et al., 2011; Petersen et al., 1999; Winblad et al., 2004). MCI affects

multiple cognitive domains, including memory, language, attention, visuospatial functioning,

speed of processing, and executive functioning (Kramer et al., 2006; Lenzi et al., 2011; Winblad

et al., 2004). MCI is also a significant public health concern, affecting 12-18% of adults over the

age of 60 (Alzheimer’s Association, 2022), and is a risk factor in progression to dementia, with

10-15% of individuals progressing to dementia within one year (Petersen et al., 2001). Given this

risk of progression, the broad impact of MCI across different cognitive domains, and the

increased need for more frequent healthcare visits with age (Zhu et al., 2013), there is a clear

need to develop and evaluate interventions that support cognitive functioning in individuals with

MCI.

Cognitive training is a non-pharmacological approach that incorporates evidence-based

strategies and skills to improve performance across cognitive domains. To date, evidence

supporting cognitive interventions for individuals with MCI has been mixed. Several systematic

reviews and meta-analyses have shown clear benefits (Belleville, 2008; Faucounau et al., 2010;

Gomez-Soria et al., 2022; Hill et al., 2017; Jean et al., 2010; Li et al., 2011; Reijnders et al.,

2013; Salzman et al., 2022), while other reviews have found little-to-no benefit (Gates et al.,

2011; Huckans et al., 2013; Kurz et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2011; Stott & Spector, 2011). The

lack of consensus on this topic is frequently attributed to methodological limitations, including


<!-- Page 5 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 4

small sample sizes, lack of appropriate control groups, and heterogeneity across interventions,

which makes comparison and synthesis across studies challenging.

Cognitive training is typically categorized into two types of approaches: restorative and

compensatory (Benedict, 1989; Ben-Yishay & Diller, 1993; Wilson, 1999). Restorative strategies

involve enhancing or restoring cognitive abilities through repeated practice of cognitive tasks

and mental exercises. In contrast, compensatory strategies are designed to teach individuals skills

and strategies for performing cognitive tasks to compensate for cognitive impairments, e.g., by

providing skills to change the way a patient learns, retains, or retrieves information.

Compensatory strategies have also been further categorized into two distinct types of strategies:

internal and external (see Table 1). External compensatory strategies involve supports such as

calendars, to-do lists, and prompts in an individual’s environment that can help improve

everyday functioning by providing tools to decrease demand on memory and facilitate task

completion (e.g., Belleville et al., 2006; Wilson, 1999). Internal compensatory strategies are

cognitive techniques that individuals can use to improve encoding of information in a

meaningful way and to improve subsequent recall, and include techniques such as categorization,

chunking, method of loci, and mental imagery (e.g., Belleville et al., 2006; Breuil et al., 1994;

Londos et al., 2008).

Despite the distinct approaches to cognitive training outlined above, many of the

interventions tested in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are not easily categorized, as several

approaches are often employed within the same intervention. These interventions are referred to

as “multicomponent” and often consist of restorative and compensatory approaches, along with

other types of interventions such as lifestyle modifications (exercise, diet changes, etc.) and

psychotherapeutic support. Cognitive training interventions are also frequently “multi-domain,”


<!-- Page 6 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 5

targeting different cognitive domains such as attention, information processing, executive

functioning, language, visuo-spatial functioning, and memory (Salzman et al., 2022; Sherman et

al., 2020). The heterogeneity of these interventions makes it difficult to isolate the specific

effects of different intervention components on improvements in patient outcomes.

However, past reviews have emphasized that cognitive interventions typically have the

largest effects on memory compared to other cognitive outcomes (e.g., Simon et al., 2012).

Furthermore, interventions specifically targeting memory have been associated with larger effect

sizes relative to multi-domain interventions (Sherman et al., 2017, 2020). A recent meta-analysis

also emphasized the efficacy of compensatory approaches to improve cognition (Sherman et al.,

2020). Compensatory strategies may be particularly effective for individuals experiencing MCI

because such strategies require deep processing of the information to be remembered (Chi &

Wylie, 2014; Menekse et al., 2013), potentially enhancing encoding and subsequent recall more

than alternative interventions. These compensatory strategies may be underpinned by

constructive learning behavior, which involves actively engaging with the material by

constructing new inferences, ideas, or connections, processes which have been shown to improve

learning outcomes (Chi et al., 2001). This is consistent with evidence demonstrating that

strategies incorporating constructive learning are more effective than non-constructive strategies

such as repetition and practicing recall of information (i.e., restorative-based approaches) (Zieve

et al., 2019). Furthermore, Milner et al. (2026) also found evidence that constructive strategies

may be more effective than non-constructive buffering against declines in memory recall in

cognitive impairment.

While recent meta-analyses have demonstrated general benefits of cognitive training on

global cognition (e.g., Gomez-Soria, 2022; Salzman et al., 2022; Sherman et al., 2020), few


<!-- Page 7 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 6

studies have focused specifically on compensatory approaches in samples that use rigorous

control groups. Given that compensatory approaches appear to be particularly effective for

individuals with MCI, there is a need for a greater focus on the most recent, rigorously designed

studies testing compensatory cognitive interventions. Therefore, the current study aims to

provide an updated meta-analysis of the literature examining the effects of compensatory

cognitive interventions exclusively in controlled studies in which patients are diagnosed with

MCI according to published criteria and objective outcomes. Furthermore, this study uses a

multi-level meta-analysis approach, which allows for retention of effect sizes for all outcomes

within a study (i.e., not averaging or creating a composite score), significantly strengthening the

validity and precision of the results.

Beyond the specific cognitive intervention components themselves, there are several

methodological characteristics of clinical trials that may also impact the magnitude of the effects.

In particular, the type of control group that is used is an important consideration for meta-

analyses, as active controls account for non-intervention effects (e.g., social engagement, time

spent) while inactive controls do not. Typically, meta-analyses find that effect sizes are greater

for studies with inactive control groups relative to active (Cuijpers et al., 2024). Furthermore,

whether the intervention is in group or individual format may influence effects. While individual

interventions may provide some benefit as they are often tailored to each patient’s needs, group

interventions may also provide some benefit through social engagement and support, which is

particularly important for individuals with MCI (Leung et al., 2015). Therefore, it’s important to

evaluate if these study-level characteristics impact the effects.

Aim 1 is to evaluate the overall efficacy of interventions incorporating compensatory

approaches on cognitive outcomes in individuals experiencing MCI. Aim 2 is to determine


<!-- Page 8 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 7

whether treatment effects of compensatory interventions vary across cognitive domains of the

outcome measure (e.g., general cognition, memory, working memory and attention, speed of

information processing, language, visual-spatial ability, executive functioning). Aim 3 is to test

the following study-level moderators on treatment effects: a) Intervention type – primarily

compensatory vs. multicomponent, b) Compensatory strategy – internal vs. external, c) Control

group type – active vs. inactive, d) Intervention format – individual vs. group.

## Method

Study Selection and Analysis

We followed the reporting guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for

Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) (Page et al., 2021) and registered the

protocol with PROSPERO (CRD420251183007) on November 23rd, 2025.

Eligibility criteria

The inclusion criteria for studies were as follows: (1) the study population was diagnosed

with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) based on established criteria (Petersen et al., 1999), (2)

the tested intervention included a compensatory component; see Table 1 for a definition of

possible compensatory components, (3) the study compared an intervention group with MCI to

an active and/or inactive control group with MCI, (4) the study included an objective,

neuropsychological outcome that assessed a cognitive domain (e.g., memory, attention), and (5)

the study reported sufficient descriptive statistics (e.g., means/SDs, effect sizes, or tests statistics)

to allow for quantitative synthesis.

Search Strategy


<!-- Page 9 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 8

Our search criteria were intended to identify cognitive interventions that included a

compensatory component in a sample diagnosed with MCI. Studies were identified by searching

the following databases: Embase, Ovid MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, and Web of Science.

The search combined three main categories of keywords using the AND and OR operators: (1)

MCI terms (e.g., “Mild Cognitive Impairment,” “MCI”); (2) Cognitive/compensatory terms:

“memory,” “compensat*,” “external aids”; (3) Intervention terms (e.g., “interven*,” “rehab*,”

“training”). The following is an example search strategy for PubMed: ("Mild Cognitive

Impairment" OR "MCI") AND ("memory" OR "compensat*" OR "cogniti*" OR "visual

imagery" OR "mental imagery" OR "method of loci" OR "mind mapping" OR "categorization"

OR "chunking" OR "cueing" OR "memory aids" OR "external aids") AND ("interven*" OR

"strateg*" OR "rehab*" OR "treatment" OR "stimulation" OR "training").

Papers were also restricted to human studies, English-language publications, and clinical

trials. The date of the last search was March 2026. Citations from each of these databases were

uploaded to Covidence, which was used for managing the review process for the meta-analysis.

Specifically, Covidence was used for detecting duplicate studies across searched databases, as

well as for conducting title and abstract screening, full-text review, data extraction, and risk of

bias assessment.

Screening

All authors served as trained reviewers who independently screened papers within

Covidence. During the initial screening phase, the title and abstract of each study were screened

by two independent reviewers. In the second phase, two independent reviewers evaluated the full

text of each paper to establish whether it met the eligibility criteria. Studies that met the


<!-- Page 10 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 9

eligibility criteria were advanced to the data extraction phase. The first author resolved conflicts

between reviewers through consensus discussions.

Data extraction

Two reviewers extracted data and categorized outcomes from the included studies, and

the first author reached a final consensus that was used in the final analyses. Data were extracted

only for objective neuropsychological outcomes and were categorized into one of the following

cognitive domains: mental status and general cognition, memory, working memory and attention,

executive function, language, speed of information processing, or visual-spatial ability. Means

and standard deviations across measures were extracted for the post-treatment time point. If data

were not collected at post-treatment, the time point closest to post-treatment was used. For

subgroup analyses, study characteristics were categorized across four study-level moderators (a)

intervention type (primarily compensatory vs. multi-component), (b) strategy type (internal vs.

external), (c) control group type (active vs. inactive), and (d) intervention format (group vs.

individual). For intervention type studies where at least half of the included components were

compensatory were classed as primarily compensatory, whereas studies in which at least one but

fewer than half of the components were compensatory were classed as multicomponent. For

strategy type, studies were classified as internal compensatory strategies if they included

mnemonic strategies, organization, categorization, mental/visual imagery, method of loci, and

face-name associations, whereas they were classed as external compensatory strategies if they

included the use of external aids or cues (e.g., calendars, notes, and prompts). For control group

type, studies were classed as active if they included an active treatment condition as a control

(e.g., treatment-as-usual, inferior treatment) or inactive (e.g., psychoeducation, waitlist control).


<!-- Page 11 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 10

For intervention format, studies where patients completed treatment alone were classed as

individual and studies where patients attended sessions with other patients were classed as group.

Risk of bias assessments

The original Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 1.0; Higgins et al., 2011) was used to

assess randomized controlled trials (RCTs) as either at high, unclear, or low risk of bias across

seven domains: (1) sequence generation, (2) allocation concealment, (3) blinding of participants

and personnel for all outcomes, (4) blinding of outcome assessors for all outcomes, (5)

incomplete outcome data for all outcomes, (6) selective outcome reporting, and (7) other sources

of bias. There were two non-randomized controlled trials (Moro et al., 2012; Mraz et al., 2023)

that were assessed with the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies (Sterne et al., 2016). The

ROBINS-I comprises seven domains that are rated as either high, moderate, or low risk: (1) bias

due to confounding, (2) bias in selection of participants into the study, (3) bias in classification of

interventions, (4) bias due to deviations from intended interventions, (5) bias due to missing data,

(6) bias in measurement of outcomes, and (7) bias in selection of the reported result.

Analysis

All analyses were performed in R (Core Team, 2021). Standardized mean differences

(SMDs) at post-treatment were used, following methodological recommendations that using

change scores can result in biased outcomes when conducting a meta-analysis on RCTs

(Chandler et al., 2019; Cuijpers et al., 2017). Effect sizes were calculated using the esc package

(Lüdecke et al., 2019), where differences in means between the intervention and control groups

at post-treatment were calculated as Hedges’ g (intervention minus control). The 95% confidence

interval (CI) was also calculated for each effect. While higher scores across most outcome

measures indicate better scores, the directionality of some outcome measures was reversed (e.g.,


<!-- Page 12 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 11

ADAS-cog, CDR-SB, TMT). These measures were multiplied by -1. Thus, positive SMDs

reflect a greater improvement in outcome for the intervention group than for the control group

across all study outcomes.

One study (Park et al., 2019) only reported change from baseline scores and standard

deviations, and the correlations between the baseline and post-treatment measures were

unknown. As recommended in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews and

Interventions (Chandler et al., 2019), the baseline SD was substituted for the post-treatment SD

when calculating effect sizes for this study, with the assumption that variability in outcomes was

not influenced by the intervention. Jeong et al. (2016) included two active interventions: an in-

person group-based intervention and a home-based intervention consisting of homework

exercises. Only values pertaining to the group-based intervention were retained when calculating

effect sizes, as this intervention included primarily compensatory strategies, whereas the home-

based intervention did not. There was only one measure of visual-spatial ability across studies

(Corsi Spatial Sequence Task; CSST). This measure was collapsed into the “working memory

and attention” domain, as it also serves as a measure of spatial working memory. Two studies

(Belleville et al., 2018; Olchik et al., 2013) included both an active and inactive control group.

For these studies, the active control was selected for the primary analysis to provide a more

conservative estimate. However, effects relative to both the active and the inactive control group

were included for the sub-group analysis examining control group type as a moderator.

Multi-level random-effects meta-analyses were conducted using the metafor package

(Viechtbauer, 2010). Models were estimated using restricted maximum-likelihood estimation

(REML). For Aim 1, the overall treatment effect of compensatory interventions across all

cognitive outcomes was evaluated using a multi-level model to account for multiple observations


<!-- Page 13 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 12

nested within each study. Level 1 accounted for the participant-level sampling error, Level 2

accounted for within-study variation (i.e., multiple outcomes reported within the same study),

and Level 3 accounted for between-study variation. This was an intercept-only model, which did

not include any predictors but was used to calculate an overall average effect size across all

outcomes. Aim 2 tested whether treatment effects differed across cognitive domain outcomes as

well as the significance of the effect associated with each type of outcome. A similar multi-level

model was run, except that Aim 2 included cognitive domain of the outcome as a moderator. One

version of the model retained the global intercept to provide an omnibus test for cognitive

domain as a moderator. A second version of the model omitting the global intercept was also run

to test whether the treatment effect associated with each cognitive domain was statistically

different from 0. For Aim 3, similar multi-level models were used to examine whether treatment

effects were moderated by four study-level characteristics: (a) intervention type (compensatory

vs. multicomponent), (b) strategy type (external vs. internal), (c) control group type (active vs.

inactive), and (d) intervention format (individual vs. group). To determine whether the impact of

these study-level characteristics also depended on the cognitive domain of the outcome, a series

of additional models was run. For each characteristic, a standard interaction model including

both the characteristic and cognitive domain as predictors was tested. One version of the models

retained the global intercept to provide omnibus tests of the interactions. A second version of the

models omitting the global intercepts was also run to determine whether each of the pooled

treatment effects associated with each of the characteristic x cognitive domain combinations was

significantly different from 0.

## Results


<!-- Page 14 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 13

Our search terms provided 2398 records after duplicates were removed. A total of 360

studies remained after title and abstract screening, and 23 studies remained after full-text review.

The main reasons for exclusion were study samples not meeting established MCI criteria and

tested interventions not including a compensatory component. See Figure 1 for the selection

process and all reasons for exclusion. Effect sizes were calculated as Hedges’ g and can be

interpreted as follows: very small (0.00-0.19), small (0.20-0.49), moderate (0.50-0.79), or large

effect (≥ 0.80) (Cohen, 2013).

Characteristics of included studies

See Table 2 for details of the 23 studies included in the meta-analysis, including study

design, sample size, descriptives (age and mental status), intervention characteristics (format,

length, components), and outcome measures. There were 21 RCTs and 2 non-randomized

controlled studies. The majority of included studies tested primarily compensatory interventions

(n = 17, 73.9%), and the remaining studies tested multicomponent interventions (n = 6, 26.1%).

Studies primarily employed internal compensatory strategies (n = 15, 65.2%); only one study

included purely external compensatory strategies (n = 1, 4.3%); and several studies employed

both internal and external strategies (n = 7, 30.4%). Different studies also used different

intervention formats, including individual sessions (n = 14, 60.9%), group sessions (n = 8,

34.8%), and both individual and group sessions (n = 1, 4.3%). Eleven studies had an inactive

control group (47.8%), ten had an active control group (43.5%), and two had both an inactive

and active control (8.7%). Studies included outcome measures from several different cognitive

domains (which were not mutually exclusive within-study): mental status and general cognition

(n = 13, 56.5%), memory (n = 20, 87.0%), working memory and attention (n = 10, 43.5%),


<!-- Page 15 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 14

executive function (n = 9, 39.1%), language (n = 5, 21.7%), and speed of information processing

(n = 7, 30.4%).

Risk of bias assessments

RCTs were assessed for risk of bias using the RoB 1.0 across seven different domains.

See Figure 2 for a summary of risk of bias across the 21 RCT studies. All studies were rated as

high risk for blinding of participants and personnel because participants and personnel could not

be blinded, which is often unavoidable in behavioral intervention studies. Most studies were

rated as low risk for sequence generation (66.7%), allocation concealment (57.1%), blinding of

outcome assessors (61.9%), incomplete outcome data (71.43%), and other sources of bias

(61.9%). Most studies had unclear risk for selective outcome reporting (61.9%) because most

studies were not pre-registered.

The two non-randomized controlled studies (Moro et al., 2012; Mraz et al., 2023) were

assessed with the ROBINS-I across seven risk domains: bias due to confounding (1 high, 1

moderate), bias in selection of participants into the study (2 low), bias in classification of

interventions (2 low), bias due to deviations from intended interventions (2 moderate), bias due

to missing data (2 low), bias in measurement of outcomes (1 moderate, 1 low), and bias in

selection of reported result (1 moderate, 1 low). Each risk of bias domain was included as a

moderator in a separate model described below (see sensitivity analyses). The lack of

participant/personnel blinding domain was not included as a moderator, as all studies were rated

as high risk.

Aim 1: Overall treatment effect of compensatory cognitive interventions

The overall pooled Hedges’ g (across all cognitive outcomes) was 0.37 (95% CI [0.23,

0.51], SE = 0.07, t(154) = 5.22, p < 0.001), indicating a moderate and positive overall effect of


<!-- Page 16 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 15

compensatory cognitive interventions. See Figure 3 for a forest plot of these effects; note that while

the full multi-level model analyzed 155 effect sizes, the plot depicts study-level composites for the

23 included studies for visual clarity. Forest plots of the 155 effect sizes are reported by cognitive

domain of the outcome in Supplement Figures S1-S6.

Total heterogeneity was moderate and statistically significant (I2 = 59.88%, Q(154) =

315.64, p < 0.001). Of the total variation, 50.28% was attributable to between-study

heterogeneity (Level 3), 9.60% to within-study heterogeneity (Level 2), and the remaining

40.13% to sampling error. The three-level model provided a significantly better fit compared to a

two-level model with level 3 heterogeneity constrained to 0 (χ21 = 41.44, p < 0.001).

Sensitivity Analyses

To evaluate whether there were any influential studies, Cook’s distance was calculated for

each study. Based on the recommended threshold of 4/n (Bollen & Jackman, 1985), two

studies—Fonte et al. (2019) and Herrera et al. (2012)—were identified as being potentially

influential because their Cook’s distance values (D = 0.18 and D = 0.23, respectively) exceeded

this threshold (0.17 for the current meta-analysis). Sensitivity analyses were conducted excluding

these two studies from the multi-level model. The point estimate of the pooled effect after

exclusion was significant (Hedges’ g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.19, 0.42], p < 0.001) and was similar to

the point estimate prior to exclusion.

Visual inspection of a funnel plot revealed patterns of asymmetry that suggested small-

study effects, whereby smaller studies are typically associated with larger effect sizes, which can

be the result of publication bias or other sources of bias. This asymmetry was further evaluated

using a multi-level model with standard error as a predictor. Larger standard errors were

associated with larger effect sizes (b = 2.62, SE = 0.51, p < 0.001), indicating that less precise


<!-- Page 17 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 16

studies reported larger effect sizes. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution

because publication bias diagnostics are not yet well established for multi-level meta-analyses.

Given the evidence of small-sample effects, sensitivity analyses excluding individual effect sizes

with a high standard error (greater than 0.40 based on visual inspection of the funnel plot) were

conducted. Following exclusion, 44 of the 155 effect sizes were excluded based on this

threshold; there was still a significant positive pooled effect estimate (g = 0.22, 95% CI [0.12,

0.33], p < 0.001), although the effect size was substantially smaller than when including all

studies (g = 0.37).

Sensitivity analyses were also conducted with the risk of bias rating for each domain, as

determined by the ROBINS-I or RoB 1.0, included as a moderator in separate models. Sequence

generation, allocation concealment, blinding of outcome assessors, incomplete outcome data, and

selective outcome reporting risk ratings did not significantly moderate outcomes. However, the

other sources of bias domain significantly moderated outcomes (F(2, 152) = 10.24, p < 0.001),

such that the studies rated as high risk for other sources of bias (i.e., baseline imbalances,

baseline differences, etc.) had larger effects than those that were rated as low risk (b = -0.53,

95% CI [-0.76, -0.30], p < 0.001). There was no significant difference between unclear and high-

risk studies (b = -0.28, 95% CI [-0.74, 0.18], p = 0.23). These results indicate that other sources

of bias may have affected the magnitude of the effects. The primary model was re-run restricted

only to studies that were rated as low-risk for other sources of bias. The pooled effect size

remained significant (g = 0.21, 95% CI [0.10, 0.31], p < 0.001), demonstrating that while high-

risk studies inflated the observed effect, the overall finding remains robust.

Aim 2: Treatment effects by domain of cognitive outcome

Compensatory Interventions for MCI 17

To evaluate whether overall treatment effects differed by cognitive domain of the

outcome, a multi-level meta-analysis was conducted with cognitive domain type as a moderator.

The overall pooled effect did not differ significantly between cognitive domains (F(5, 149) =

1.53, p = 0.18), suggesting that outcomes across domains were comparable. As a descriptive

analysis, a multi-level model omitting the global intercept was conducted to assess whether the

effect size for each cognitive domain outcome was significantly different from zero. There was a

statistically significant effect of the interventions on mental status and general cognition (g =

0.31, 95% CI [0.13, 0.50], p < 0.01), memory (g = 0.43, 95% CI [0.27, 0.58], p < 0.001),

working memory and attention (g = 0.44, 95% CI [0.25, 0.62], p < 0.001), executive functioning

(g = 0.28, 95% CI [0.05, 0.51], p = 0.02), and language (g = 0.29, 95% CI [0.06, 0.52], p = 0.01).

Intervention effects on the speed of information processing were not significant (g = 0.21, 95%

CI [-0.04, 0.45], p = 0.10). See Figure 4 for a forest plot of the estimated pooled effects by

cognitive domain.

Aim 3: Sub-group analyses

In our pre-registered protocol, we planned to conduct sub-group analyses to examine

potential moderation effects across several variables: MCI subtype (amnestic, non-amnestic),

compensatory strategy type (internal, external), control group type (active, inactive control), and

intervention format (individual, group, both). The majority of the included studies examined

individuals with amnestic MCI (n = 14), and the remaining studies did not specify whether their

samples included amnestic or non-amnestic individuals. Therefore, the planned sub-group

analyses for MCI subtype were not conducted. Furthermore, only a single study included a

purely external compensatory approach (Greenaway et al., 2013). Therefore, the pre-registered

analysis of compensatory strategies was adapted to instead compare studies that included only


<!-- Page 19 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 18

internal strategies (n = 15) to interventions including external strategies (n = 1 external only; n =

7 internal and external). Only one study (Schmitter-Edgecombe & Dyck, 2014) included both a

group and individual format. Thus, this study was excluded from the intervention format sub-

group analyses. Additionally, a post-hoc exploratory analysis was conducted to test the effects of

intervention type (primarily compensatory vs. multicomponent). The sub-group analyses

involving intervention type, compensatory strategy approach, control group type, and

intervention format are reported below.

Aim 3a: Treatment effects by intervention approach (compensatory only versus

multicomponent)

To evaluate whether overall treatment effects differed by the intervention approach across

all cognitive outcomes combined, a multi-level meta-analysis was conducted with intervention

type as a moderator. The overall pooled effect did not differ significantly between primarily

compensatory and multicomponent interventions (b = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.28, 0.36], p  = 0.81),

suggesting that effect sizes for compensatory (g = 0.37) and multicomponent interventions (g =

0.40) were comparable. To determine whether the difference in treatment effects between the two

intervention types varied by cognitive domain of the outcome, another similar multi-level

## Discussion

The primary goal of this meta-analysis was to examine the impact of cognitive

interventions that include compensatory strategies on outcomes in individuals with MCI and to

examine potential moderators of these effects. Specifically, the first aim evaluated the overall

impact of these interventions across all cognitive outcomes. There was a small-to-moderate


<!-- Page 24 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 23

effect size (g = 0.37) across outcomes. This finding suggests that, in general, individuals with

MCI who are taught compensatory strategies show improvements in cognition.

The second aim evaluated whether treatment effects were moderated by the cognitive

domain of the outcome measure (i.e., general cognition and mental status, memory, working

memory and attention, language, and speed of processing). Although effect sizes did not differ

significantly between cognitive domains, the largest improvements were observed in memory (g

= 0.43) and working memory/attention (g = 0.44). There were also small effects on mental status

and general cognition (g = 0.31), executive functioning (g = 0.28), and language outcomes (g =

0.29), but no significant effect of the interventions on speed of processing (g = 0.21). These

findings indicate that cognitive compensatory interventions provide benefits across most

cognitive outcomes for individuals with MCI. Specifically, they yield the greatest efficacy for

memory and working memory/attention outcomes, but they appear not to be effective for speed

of processing outcomes. It’s plausible that compensatory strategies, which are designed to reduce

demands on limited cognitive resources (Clare & Woods, 2004) rather than directly remediate

underlying cognition, are unlikely to result in improvements for speed of information processing.

This interpretation is consistent with evidence suggesting that restorative cognitive interventions,

which employ repetitive, task-specific training to enhance or restore cognitive function, can have

moderate effects on speed of information processing in samples without MCI (Lampit et al.,

2019). Unlike compensatory approaches, restorative interventions target underlying cognitive

mechanisms via repeated practice and more direct focus on processing speed, attention, memory,

and executive function (Hardy & Scanlon, 2009; Westerberg et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2019). A

valuable domain for future research is to determine if restorative approaches may be better suited


<!-- Page 25 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 24

to address the cognitive domains for which compensatory interventions failed to yield significant

effects in patients with MCI.

The third aim was to evaluate whether treatment effects differed by the following

subgroups: a) intervention type, b) compensatory strategy, c) control group type, and d)

intervention format. Aim 3a evaluated the type of intervention approach that was used by testing

intervention approach (primarily compensatory vs. multicomponent with at least one

compensatory component) as a moderator. There were no significant differences between the two

intervention approaches when collapsing across outcomes, and the results of the omnibus

interaction model testing both intervention and cognitive domain as moderators were not

significant. The lack of a moderation effect for the pooled results indicates that neither

intervention type is superior to the other when evaluating cognitive outcomes overall. From a

clinical perspective, this indicates there may be some flexibility in the type of approach used

based on resources, patient preference, and clinical expertise without influencing the efficacy of

the intervention. However, when examining individual cognitive domains, distinct underlying

processes may dictate which intervention types provide the greatest benefit.

The two intervention types were comparable for memory (g = 0.43 and 0.44 for

multicomponent and compensatory interventions, respectively) and for mental status and general

cognition (g = 0.32 and 0.33, respectively). However, while the effect of multicomponent

interventions was significant for executive functioning (g = 0.47) and approached significance

for speed of information processing (g = 0.30), there was no significant effect for compensatory

interventions on executive functioning (g = 0.19) or on speed of information processing (g =

0.02). Multicomponent interventions also showed larger effects than compensatory interventions

on working memory/attention (g = 0.67 vs. 0.37, respectively), although both effects were


<!-- Page 26 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 25

significant. These results suggest that while purely compensatory approaches are most beneficial

for mental status/general cognition and memory, multicomponent interventions may target a

broader range of cognitive abilities, including working memory, executive function, and speed of

information processing. This may be because most multicomponent interventions employ a

combination of restorative and compensatory approaches, in which restorative interventions

primarily target domains such as processing speed, attention, and executive function (Hardy &

Scanlon, 2009; Westerberg et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2019). This distinction has important

clinical implications for designing interventions. Patients with amnestic MCI, which is primarily

characterized by impairments in memory, may benefit most from compensatory interventions,

while non-amnesic MCI can result in impairments in attention/concentration, information

processing, language, and executive function (Luck et al., 2010; Petersen et al., 2009), which

may be better targeted by restorative approaches. Unfortunately, the included studies did not

allow for the analysis of MCI subtype, which will be important to establish in future work.

Aim 3b was to evaluate whether treatment effects differed by the type of compensatory

strategy employed, comparing internal strategies (e.g., mental imagery, mnemonics) to external

strategies (e.g., calendars, cues, and prompts). Collapsing across cognitive outcomes, there was

no significant difference in treatment effects between internal and external strategies (g = 0.35

for internal, g = 0.42 for external). However, when examining the effects on outcomes from

different cognitive domains, there was a significant effect of internal (g = 0.35) but not external

strategies (g = 0.20) on mental status and general cognition. Treatment effects were generally

larger for external compared to internal approach across the following cognitive domains:

memory (g = 0.60 vs. 0.36), working memory and attention (g = 0.53 vs. 0.41), and language (g

= 0.40 vs. 0.25). This indicates that external strategies may be effective at targeting more


<!-- Page 27 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 26

cognitive domains. However, more research needs to be conducted on interventions that evaluate

each of these strategy types in isolation and specifically in individuals experiencing MCI.

Aim 3c was to evaluate whether treatment effects differed depending on the type of

control group used, comparing inactive (did not receive any treatment) to active (received active

treatment, e.g., treatment-as-usual, alternative intervention) control groups. Overall, effect sizes

were not significantly different for studies with active (g = 0.44) compared to inactive control

groups (g = 0.31). However, the point estimates of effect sizes were larger for studies including

an active control than for those with an inactive for mental status and cognition (g = 0.48 vs.

0.15), memory (g = 0.49 vs. 0.34), working memory and attention (g = 0.59 vs. 0.32), executive

functioning (g = 0.62 vs. -0.01), and speed of information processing (g = 0.33 vs. 0.06). These

findings are surprising, given that effect sizes are usually larger in studies with inactive controls

than in those with active controls (Cuijpers et al., 2024). It is possible that there was a higher

dropout rate in the inactive control condition, as participants knew that they were not receiving

treatment, which may have contributed to smaller effects by introducing attrition bias, whereby

patients with lower baseline functioning—who may benefit the most from treatment—

disproportionately dropped out from the control group. Active control trials are more likely to be

real-world or later stage and may have higher baseline severity, which can lead to greater room

for improvement, resulting in larger pre- to post changes for these individuals.

Aim 3d examined whether the intervention format (individual versus group) impacted

treatment effects. There was no significant difference between individual and group interventions

when examining pooled treatment effects. However, the point estimate of the effect size for the

group format (g = 0.50) was qualitatively larger than for the individual format (g = 0.31). The

results of the analysis examining cognitive outcome and format as moderators approached


<!-- Page 28 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 27

significance (p = 0.09). The point estimates of the treatment effects were larger for group formats

relative to individual for the following cognitive outcomes: mental status and cognition (g = 0.58

vs. 0.16), memory (g = 0.57 vs. 0.37), executive functioning (g = 0.46 vs. 0.17). This finding

indicates that group formats may be better for select cognitive outcomes for individuals with

MCI. Past research examining the effects of group versus individual interventions has yielded

mixed findings, with some research evaluating psychological therapies finding no difference

(McRoberts et al., 1998), while others have shown greater benefits for individual formats

(Cuijpers et al., 2008; Huntley et al., 2012). Similarly, mixed outcomes have been found in

patient populations with dementia (Woods et al., 2012), and one study found that group settings

were particularly effective at improving memory outcomes for midlife and older adults in

residential care settings (Haslam et al., 2010). This may be in line with the findings of the current

meta-analysis, suggesting that the social aspect of group interventions can play an important role

in health and well-being in midlife and older adults, including those with MCI.

There are several limitations to this meta-analysis. First, several sub-group analyses had

small and unbalanced group sizes, which may have reduced the statistical power to detect true

differences between them. Second, even within subgroups, there was a high degree of

heterogeneity across studies (i.e., different types of interventions used), making it difficult to

isolate independent effects of specific strategies. There were also not enough instances of some

variable levels of interest to justify including them in analysis. For example, only a single study

evaluated a purely external strategy approach, so we were unable to evaluate the effectiveness of

external strategies alone. Future research is needed to specifically test each of these strategy

types or evaluate their effects in isolation. Finally, diagnostic assessments revealed significant

evidence of small-study effects and publication bias, where smaller studies (assumed to have less


<!-- Page 29 -->


Compensatory Interventions for MCI 28

precision) reported larger effect sizes. Although a sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the

pooled treatment effect was still statistically significant after excluding studies with large

standard errors, the effect size did drop from g = 0.37 to g = 0.22, implying that the true effect

size may be lower (i.e., in the small range) than suggested in the main analysis.

This meta-analysis evaluated RCTs measuring the effectiveness of cognitive interventions

with a compensatory component for improving cognitive outcomes in patients with MCI. Results

showed that treatment effects were in the small-to-moderate range across cognitive outcomes.

The interventions in the included studies had the largest effects on memory and working

memory/attention outcomes. Interestingly, there was some evidence that, when compared to

primarily compensatory approaches, multicomponent interventions (i.e., those that were partly

compensatory but more heavily restorative) were better for improving certain cognitive

processes, including working memory/attention, executive functioning, and speed of information

processing. In some cases, there was also evidence that external strategies were more effective

than internal strategies and that interventions were more effective when delivered in a group

setting than when delivered individually.

# A frameshift mutation drives divergent biosynthesis of metallophores in Methylobacterium extorquens

**Authors:** Alexa M Zytnick; Marquis T Yazzie; Tashi CE Liebergesell; Elan H Tran; Zachary L Reitz; Aaron W Puri; Allegra T Aron; Norma Cecilia Martinez-Gomez

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Plant and Microbial Biology, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA | 2Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of Denver, Denver, CO, USA | 3Department of Chemistry and the Henry Eyring Center for Cell and Genome Science, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA | 4Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Marine Biology, University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, CA, USA

## Abstract

Iron is widely considered the first metallocofactor, evolving as iron-sulfur clusters in early life. While iron-chelating siderophores have been widely characterized across microbial life, the lanthanide-chelating metallophore, methylolanthanin, has only recently been described in Methylobacterium extorquens AM1. Methylolanthanin shares structural similarities to the siderophore rhodopetrobactin but contains 4-hydroxybenzoate chelating moieties in place of canonical 3,4-dihydroxybenzoates. Here we compare M. extorquens AM1, which produces methylolanthanin, and the closely related M. extorquens PA1, which produces rhodopetrobactin. We present a pathway for the biosynthesis of both metallophores and describe the unusual synthesis of methylolanthanin’s 4-HB moieties from tyrosine. We uncover a frameshift mutation in the predicted 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase, mllF, that prevents production of rhodopetrobactin in AM1 through truncation of the catalytically essential N-terminus. We find that deletion of the uncharacterized gene mllG reveals a cryptic branch of the pathway, leading to production of both methylolanthanin and rhodopetrobactin. Finally, we discover that rhodopetrobactin production in this mutant is enabled through the activity of a 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase in a separate biosynthetic gene cluster. These insights highlight an evolutionary mechanism for metallophore diversification through pseudogenization and regulation of distinct biosynthetic gene clusters with shared aromatic intermediates.

## Introduction

Metals are essential for a wide range of biological processes, from acting as signals in regulatory cascades to stabilizing DNA structure.1–3 Metals also play key catalytic and structural roles within the majority of enzymes.3 While the biological importance of transition metals has been extensively studied, the f-block lanthanides have only recently been discovered as biologically relevant metals. XoxF, a methanol dehydrogenase from methylotrophic bacteria, was the first enzyme to be classified as lanthanide-dependent. Since XoxF’s discovery, the field of lanthanide biology has been steadily growing, with additional lanthanide-dependent alcohol dehydrogenases from both methylotrophic and non-methylotrophic organisms being discovered.4–6

One way metals such as lanthanides are acquired is through the secretion of small molecule metallophores. This is a well-established strategy across various microorganisms, with iron-chelating siderophores and copper-chelating chalkophores playing essential ecological roles in host-pathogen and plant environments.7–9 These secondary metabolites are built by elegant biosynthetic complexes, such as non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPS) or NRPS-polyketide synthases (PKS) hybrids. Some microbial siderophores have been characterized to be NRPS independent and are instead derived from dicarboxylic acid and diamine or amino alcohol units.10

Recently, it was discovered that methylolanthanin (MLL) is a lanthanide chelator produced by the model methylotroph Methylobacterium extorquens AM1 via an NRPS-independent pathway in response to the limitation of bioavailable lanthanides (Fig. 1A).11 MLL is a citrate based metallophore, with 4-hydroxybenzoate (4-HB) moieties and acetylated homospermidine arms. MLL’s unique 4-HB moiety precludes the molecule’s classification into the traditional chemical groups of metallophores: catecholates, phenolates, hydroxamates, carboxylates, or diazeniumdiolates. This moiety is also the key structural difference between methylolanthanin and the catecholate siderophore rhodopetrobactin (RPB) (Fig. 1B).12 Interestingly, MLL is not a biological intermediate of RPB, despite its production in response to iron limitation, as the catechol groups of Bacillus anthracis Sterne’s petrobactin originate from the direct dehydration of 3-dehydroshikimate to 3,4-dihydroxybenzoate.13

Methylobacterium extorquens PA1 robustly produces RPB (Fig. 1A, B).14 We take advantage of this finding as well as the fact that M. extorquens AM1 does not produce RPB to compare the biosynthetic routes to these two metallophores. Individual mll knockouts in AM1 revealed essential, nonessential, and putative regulatory proteins in the production of MLL. From these data, we present a proposal for the biosynthesis of MLL and RPB, with the aromatic precursor origin controlling the output of the mll BGC. From inverse stable isotopic labeling (InverSIL) experiments, we present the biosynthesis of these aromatic precursors, describing the unique production of methylolanthanin’s 4-HB from tyrosine. Through multiple sequence alignments, protein structure prediction, and the production of genetic mutants, we show the 3-dehdryoshikimate dehydratase in the mll cluster is dispensable for MLL and RPB biosynthesis, suggesting that pseudogenization of this biosynthetic enzyme allowed for metallophore diversification. Finally, we characterize a mutant that produces both MLL and RPB through utilizing an active 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase from a different locus. Together, these findings reveal the mechanistic basis of divergent metallophore production from very similar biosynthetic gene clusters.

## Results

### Mutagenesis reveals the function of biosynthetic genes essential for MLL production

To investigate the biosynthesis of MLL, individual deletions of each biosynthetic gene (mllA, mllBC, mllDE, mllF, mllG, mllH, and mllJ) were made in a ΔmxaF background. Mutants were grown in minimal media with methanol as a carbon substrate and supplemented with NdCl3 or Nd2O3. Supernatant extracts were analyzed via non-targeted metabolomics using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC– MS/MS).

mllF, mllG, and mllJ were found to be dispensable for MLL production (Fig. 2A), while mllA, mllBC, and mllDE were found to be essential for MLL production (Fig. 2B), consistent with biosynthetic analysis of the petrobactin pathway from Bacillus anthracis Sterne.15,16 Using petrobactin biosynthesis as a model, we hypothesized MllA to catalyze the addition of 4-HB-homospermidine (1) to citrate to form 4-HB-homospermidine-citrate (2). MllBC is hypothesized to catalyze the condensation of homospermidine or another 4-HB-homospermidine to 4-HB-homospermidine-citrate to produce the symmetric intermediate di-N-citrylhomospermidine (3) or the asymmetric intermediate 4-HB-homospermidine-citrate (4) (MllB) coupled to the transfer of 4-HB to a phosphopantetheine group attached to MllD (MllC). MllDE is hypothesized to condense 4-HB-loaded MllD with its substrates (3) or (4). Finally, MllH is hypothesized to transfer acetyl groups onto amines to produce the final metallophore.

Interestingly, 4-HB-putrescene was one of the most differentially abundant features between the mllA and the mllBC deletions (Fig. S1A). While not the hypothesized 4-HB-homospermidine, the absence of 4-HB-putrescene in ΔmllBC and ΔmllDE is consistent with the proposed functions of MllBCDE in activating and condensing 4-HB. Interestingly, MllF was found to be required for 4-HB-putrescene production (Fig. 2B and Fig. S1B). Additionally, it has been reported that 4-HB-homospermidine is difficult to detect via MS.16 We also do not detect 4-HB-homospermidine-citrate (2) in any samples because MllA is predicated to catalyze this reaction and the MllBC and MllDE fusions are necessary to produce the 4-HB-homospermidine precursor of (2).

Intermediate (3) was not found in ΔmllA and ΔmllBC but was found in ΔmllDE (Fig. 2B), which highlights the role of mllDE in 4-HB ligation. Deletion of mllH resulted in intermediates lacking acetyl groups, confirming its proposed role as an N-acetyltransferase (Fig. 2B and Fig. S9). Due to their co-upregulation with the mll cluster, META1p5050 and META1p5051 were identified as potential hydroxylases and decarboxylases acting upon the aromatic precursor of 4-HB, but deletion of either gene still yielded MLL production (Fig. S2).

### Inverse labeling towards elucidating the origin of 4-hydroxybenzoate

As the key difference between MLL and RPB is the replacement of two 3,4-DHB moieties with 4-HB moieties, the origin of 4-HB was investigated through utilizing InverSIL.17 The ΔmllF mutant, which produces only MLL (Fig. 2A), was grown in minimal media with 13C-substituted methanol as a carbon source and supplemented with unlabeled putative aromatic intermediates to detect for incorporation via LC-HRMS/MS. Interestingly, when precursors that are eventually incorporated are added, MLL is produced in much greater amounts than the wildtype, suggesting aromatic precursors are in limited supply.

AM1 does not contain a UbiC homolog, which converts chorismate to 4-HB, and would be the assumed source of this aromatic precursor for MLL. A novel pathway for the biosynthesis of 4-HB in Klebsiella oxytoca was characterized to originate from tyrosine, proceeding through 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, 4-hydroxyphenyllactate, 4-hydroxymandelate, 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde, with a final oxidation to 4-HB.18 Through inverse labeling we see incorporation of each of these intermediates from this pathway into MLL, from tyrosine to 4-HB, apart from 4-hydroxyphenyllactate (Fig. 3, Table S1).

### Nonessential mll genes control alternative aromatic precursor routing and regulation

The production of methylolanthanin by mllF, mllG, and mllJ deletion mutants (Fig. 2A) led us to investigate the roles of their protein products. MllF is annotated as a sugar phosphate isomerase/epimerase family protein and shares similarity with the 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase AsbF from petrobactin producer Bacillus anthracis Sterne.15 A blastn search of mllF against RefSeq genomes showed nucleotide sequence similarity to other AsbF homologs across methylotrophs, including PA1. A multiple sequence alignment of AsbF homologs from AM1, PA1, and Methylorubrum aminovorans NBRC 15686 revealed frameshift mutations in AM1 and M. aminovorans NBRC 15686 that are absent in PA1 and other methylotrophs (Fig. 4A). These frameshifts truncate the canonical N-terminus of the protein, however, a downstream in-frame start codon is predicted to permit expression of a folded core protein.

AlphaFold modeling of MllF, homologs from PA1 and M. aminovorans NBRC 15686, overlaid with the crystal structure of AsbF from Bacillus anthracis Sterne reveal that AsbF and its PA1 homolog share a matching N-terminal beta sheet and loop at the dimer interface (Fig. 4B), interactions that are documented as essential for activity in this family of enzymes.19 The homologous proteins in AM1 and M. aminovorans NBRC 15686 lack one or both of these N terminal features due to the truncation caused by the aforementioned frameshift mutations (Fig. 4A, B). This leads to catalytically inactive forms of these enzymes, explaining the lack of production of RPB in AM1 and the capacity of the AM1 mllF deletion mutant to still produce MLL (Fig. 2A). We verify that the misfolded N-terminus of mllF is the cause of MLL production through heterologously expressing the PA1 mllF homolog in a ΔmllF background in AM1 (Fig. 2D). We find that expression of the active enzyme from PA1, Mext3763, leads to the production of RPB instead of MLL (Fig. 4D). While M. extorquens AM1 does not naturally produce RPB under the tested conditions, deletion of mllG when grown under Nd2O3 led to production of RPB in addition to the production of MLL (Fig. 2B and Fig. S5). We find that production of RPB is conferred through the activity of a putative 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase, META1p2877, that is located in a locus outside of the mll cluster. META1p2877 is predicted to retain a folded N-terminus and therefore remain active (Fig. 4C). Deletion of META1p2877 in a mllG deletion background abolished the single mutant’s capacity to produce RPB, denoting that META1p2877 is responsible for the production of the 3,4-DHB incorporated into RPB produced by the mllG single mutant (Fig. 4D). In addition, the deletion of META1p2877 had no significant effect on the relative abundance of MLL (Fig 4D).

## Discussion

Iron is considered one of the oldest metallocofactors.20–22 Lanthanide dependent enzymes and systems for lanthanide uptake likely evolved much later than iron enzymes and uptake systems. During the Phanerozoic to modern eras, acidic environments and terrestrial weathering made lanthanides more available, and even produced Fe-oxyhydroxides that acted as sinks for light lanthanides.23–26 Here, we present insights into the evolution of lanthanide and iron metallophores in M. extorquens AM1 and M. extorquens PA1. Simultaneous work from Gutenthaler-Tietze et al has corroborated the production of MLL in AM1, RPB in PA1, and the presence of the frameshift in the AsbF homolog MllF.27

We find the biosynthesis of the cores of RPB and MLL proceed similarly to that of the siderophore petrobactin, but with homospermidine instead of spermidine. We find MllBC and MllDE are likely necessary to produce 4-HB-homospermidine from 4-HB and homospermidine (Fig. 5). While MllA is predicted to then catalyze the addition of citrate to 4-HB-homospermidine, 2, this intermediate was not detected. This may be due to the MllBC and MllDE fusions, in contrast to their standalone homologs in the petrobactin biosynthesis pathway (AsbB, AsbC, AsbD, and AsbE).16 Interestingly, the RPB biosynthetic gene cluster from Rhodospeduomonas palustris TIE-1 exhibits an intermediate fusion phenotype, as it possesses independent AsbB and AsbC homologs but an AsbDE fusion.12 Separation of these genes in the mll cluster would be necessary to detect 2, as they are necessary to produce its 4-HB-homospermidine precursor. This suggests that metallophore diversification within the petrobactin-like family may be accompanied by progressive fusion of biosynthetic enzymes.

We find MllBC to then condense another 4-HB-homospermidine to the citrate core, forming MLL, 5. Alternatively, we find another branch of MLL biosynthesis to be active, in which MllDE catalyzes the addition of a second 4-HB to 4, an intermediate that is only mono-substituted with 4-HB. We find 4 to originate from dihomospermidine-citrate, 3, which is congruent with previously described asymmetric petrobactin biosynthesis, although we do not detect the earlier intermediates from this branch of the pathway. We confirm that MllH is responsible for N-acetylation (Fig. S9) and find mono-, di-, and tri-acetylated versions of 4 and 3.

The AsbF homolog, MllF, and the uncharacterized proteins MllJ and MllG were not found to be essential for MLL production (Fig. 2A). MllF was found to be essential for the production of 4-HB-putrescine (Fig. 2B), which is structurally similar but distinct from the polyamine catechol siderophore aminochelin (2,3-DHB-putrescine).28 Dating back to the ancestral stock of M. extorquens AM1 from 1960,29 mllF exhibits a frameshift mutation that renders its protein product inactive (Fig. 4A). Heterologous expression of its functional homolog from PA1 allowed for production of RPB over MLL without restoring 4-HB-putrescine production (Fig. 4D, Fig. S1B). AM1 has seemingly evolved away from the canonical RPB biosynthetic strategy by eliminating the need for AsbF-dependent, 3-dehydroshikimate dehydratase activity. As a consequence, MllF has lost its catalytic function but has been retained because it performs a new role in an MLL-associated aromatic polyamine pathway. Within this framework, MllF does not function as a source of 4-HB but rather as a pseudoenzyme that promotes efficient flux through the MLL-producing branch. Deletion of mllF therefore reduces, but does not abolish, MLL production (Fig. 2A) while completely eliminating detectable 4-HB-putrescine (Fig. 2B), a phenotype expected if 4-HB-putrescine is a shunt product or overflow metabolite rather than an obligate precursor. The ability of a catalytically active PA1 MllF homolog to restore RPB production but not 4-HB-putrescine production (Fig. S1) further supports the idea that active AsbF chemistry drives the ancestral RPB pathway, whereas the inactive AM1 MllF has been repurposed for a distinct function associated with 4-HB-polyamines and MLL biosynthesis.

We investigate the origin of MLL’s chelating moieties via InverSIL. We find that 4-HB is incorporated into MLL, is not incorporated into RPB, and that 4-HB originates from tyrosine and not from canonical catechol biosynthesis pathways (Fig. 3). 4-HB is produced from tyrosine via a novel route through 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, 4-hydroxymandelate, and 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde (Fig. 5). While no annotated 4-HPP dioxygenase was found in the AM1 genome, it has been reported that 4-HPP can be converted to 4-HBA bioinorganically with iron(IV)-oxido and iron(III)-hydroxido species.30 AM1 likely then converts 4-HBA to 4-HB through an unspecific aldehyde dehydrogenase, as subsets of this enzyme family has been shown to be promiscuous towards aromatic substrates.31

Lastly, we find that RPB and MLL may be linked evolutionarily through regulation, as DUF genes mllJ and mllG are not biosynthetically essential for production of MLL and because the mllG deletion produces both RPB and MLL (Fig. 2A). Indeed, we find that MllG may control RPB production through recruiting an AsbF homolog in a distant locus, META1p2877, for 3,4-DHB production, as a double deletion of META1p2877 and mllG fails to produce RPB (Fig. 4D). As PA1 also has mllJ and mllG (Fig. 1A), they may serve as regulatory switches to control the flow of aromatic intermediates to either RPB biosynthesis or other pathways. Interestingly MllG shows structural similarity to the uncharacterized protein PA4090 from Pseudomonas aeruginosa that was found to be differentially expressed in response to iron and the production of the siderophore pyoverdine.32 Coupled with the knowledge that the MLL cluster is responsive to iron concentrations,11 MllG may further play a role in regulating the production of RPB over MLL in iron limiting conditions. Future work that evaluates the relationship between these proteins will surely provide more insights into the regulatory network underlying metallophore diversity and biosynthesis.

## Materials and Methods

### General Working and Culturing Conditions

MilliQ grade water and HPLC grade solvents were used in this work, unless otherwise stated. For mass spectrometry and related experiments, LCMS grade solvents were used. Culturing occurred under sterile conditions. M. extorquens AM1 strains [ΔmxaF, ΔmxaFΔmll,11 ΔmxaFΔmllA, ΔmxaFΔmllBC, ΔmxaFΔmllDE, ΔmxaFΔmllF, ΔmxaFΔmllG, and ΔmxaFΔmllH, ΔmxaFΔmllJ, ΔmxaFΔMETA1p2877, ΔmxaF/pMext3763, ΔmxaFΔMETA1p5050, and ΔmxaFΔMETA1p5051] were grown in MP medium.33 3 mL cultures with 15 mM succinate (MilliporeSigma) were grown overnight in 15 mL round bottom glass culture tubes (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 30°C and 200 rpm and then diluted into the desired volume of 50 mL of fresh MP to an OD600 of 0.1. Bulk cultures were grown with 50 mM MeOH as a carbon source and 2 μM NdCl3 or Nd2O3 as lanthanide sources. When necessary, sucrose, and kanamycin were added to final concentrations of 5%, 50 μg/mL, and 50 μg/mL, respectively. The above conditions were used unless otherwise noted.

### DNA Manipulation

All fragments were amplified with either Q5 DNA polymerase or Phusion DNA polymerase (New England Biolabs). The Mext3763 overexpression vector pAZ05 was generated using Q5 polymerase to amplify fragments from PA1 gDNA and the pTE1877 backbone and these fragments were digested and ligated together using restriction enzymes and T4 ligase (New England Biolabs).34 Deletion vectors were generated by amplifying a pCM433kanT backbone and ~500 bp flanking regions upstream and downstream of target genes from AM1 gDNA. Fragments for individual mll BGC deletions and the META1p2877 deletion were fused using Gibson Assembly Master Mix (New England Biolabs). Constructs were transformed into electrocompetent DH5α or 10β E. coli (New England Biolabs), plated on selective media, and purified using the GeneJET Plasmid Miniprep Kit (Thermo Fischer Scientific). For deletion vectors, counterselection was achieved through patching transformants onto Hypho33 succinate sucrose and Hypho succinate kanamycin plates and selecting colonies with a successful double crossover event (growth on sucrose, no growth on kanamycin). Full plasmid sequencing or PCR product sequencing (Plasmidsaurus) confirmed the sequence of all constructs and the deletion of target genes.

### Bioinformatic Analysis of ORFs and Protein Structure

Biosynthetic gene cluster comparisons were constructed using clinker.35 A NCBI blastn search against RefSeq genomes was used to compile a list of mllF homologs.36,37 Alternative ORFs for mllF were discovered using NCBI ORFfinder with AM1’s genome (RefSeq accession NC_012808). Protein structures were predicted using the AlphaFold 3 server.38 Multiple sequence alignments were performed using Clustal Omega.39,40

### Mass spectrometry analysis of AM1 biosynthesis mutants for MLL, RPB and biosynthetic intermediates

Samples were received and processed in three separate batches: batch 1 contained all mll mutants ( ΔmllA, ΔmllBC, ΔmllDE, ΔmllF, ΔmllG, ΔmllH, ΔmllJ and ΔmxaF); batch 2 contained ΔmllF, ΔmllG, ΔmllJ, ΔMETA1p5050, and ΔMETA1p5051; batch 3 contained ΔmllF, ΔmllG, ΔmllF/pMext3763, and ΔmllG ΔMETA1p2877. Detailed descriptions of each batch are provided on Github. All M. extorquens AM1 strains were pelleted at 5,000 x g for ten minutes prior to shipment of supernatant at −80 °C. Once thawed, 25-50 mL of supernatant were subjected to solid phase extraction (SPE) using Chromabond HLB sorbents and a protocol aligned with the package insert. Briefly, HLB columns were conditioned with methanol then equilibrated with 3% MeOH in water prior to loading supernatant onto the column. The column was washed with 3% MeOH in water, dried with vacuum, and then eluted with 80% methanol in water. Samples were concentrated then resuspended in 200 μL of 80% methanol with 1μM sulfadimethoxine as the internal standard (batches 1 and 3). Samples in batch 2 were reconstituted to 1mg/mL based on dry sample biomass. For samples in batches 2 and 3, 1μM sulfamethazine was added as an extraction standard prior to SPE.

2-5 μL of sample was injected into a Vanquish coupled to a Q Exactive HF quadrupole orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). A Waters Acquity C18 UPLC HSS T3 1.8μm 2.1x100mm was used for chromatography. The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (water +0.1% formic acid (FA)) and solvent B (acetonitrile + 0.1% FA). The flow rate was set to 0.5 mL/min. After injection, the samples were eluted with the following method: 0 to 6 min 2% to 50% B, 6 to 10 min 50 to 99% B, followed by a 3 min washout phase at 99% B and a 3-min re-equilibration phase at 2% B. After 10 minutes from the start of the run, the divert valve switched to divert the LC flow from MS to waste. Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) of MS/MS spectra was performed in positive electrospray ionization mode. Full MS was collected with 120,000 resolution, 1e6 automatic gain control target, maximum injection time 100ms for the 150 to 1500 m/z range. The dd-MS2 was collected with 15,000 resolution, 5e5 automatic gain control target, maximum injection time 200ms, TopN 5, isolation window 1.0 m/z, and normalized collision energy stepped 25, 35 and 45. A QC mixture containing sulfamethazine, sulfamethizole, sulfachloropyridazine, sulfadimethoxine, and coumarin-314 was run every ten samples, along with method blanks.

### Feature Finding and Feature Based Molecular Networking

Profile spectra (.raw) were converted to .mzML files using MSconvert. mzmine (4.7.29) was used to detect features across batches 1 & 2, and mzmine (4.9.14) was used for batch 3. All mzmine processing files and parameters can be found in Github. GNPS2 Feature Based Molecular Networking (FBMN) was used for all data visualization and can be accessed at the following links: https://gnps2.org/status?task=4cdb0a26b5d94b258b83629ab2ad9eb6 (batch 1: presence/abscence of MLL, RPB and biosynthetic intermediates across BGC mutants); https://gnps2.org/status?task=673f01deb5c1428588495bba2c630725 (batch 2: relative abundance of MLL across ΔmllF, ΔmllG, ΔmllJ); https://gnps2.org/status?task=8236c5b380d1425293d7517c3d42d93a (batch 3: relative abundance of MLL and RPB across ΔmllF, ΔmllG, ΔmllF/pMext3763, and ΔmllG ΔMETA1p2877). Batch 1 (presence/absence of MLL, RPB and biosynthetic intermediates) was blank subtracted and imputed, and normalized, as previously described.41 Batch 2 (relative abundance of MLL across ΔmllF, ΔmllG, ΔmllJ, ΔMETA1p5050, and ΔMETA1p5051) was not blank subtracted or imputed.

### Inverse Labeling and Detection of Methylolanthanin and Rhodopetrobactin

Exponentially growing cultures were pelleted at 4,000 rpm for ten minutes and resuspended in fresh ammonium mineral salts (AMS) medium with no carbon source. Modified AMS contains 0.2 g L−1 MgSO4·7H2O, 0.2 g L−1 CaCl2·6H2O, 0.5 g L−1 NH4Cl, 30 μM LaCl3, and 1X trace elements. 500X trace elements contains 1.0 g L−1Na2-EDTA, 2.0 g L−1 FeSO4·7H2O, 0.8 g L1 ZnSO4·7H2O, 0.03 g L−1 MnCl2·4H2O, 0.03 g L−1 H3BO3, 0.2 g L−1CoCl2·6H2O, 0.6 g L1 CuCl2·2H2O, 0.02 g L−1 NiCl2·6H2O, and 0.05 g L−1 Na2Mo·2H2O. A final concentration of 4 mM phosphate buffer pH 6.8 and 50 mM 12C- or 13C-methanol were added prior to use. Subsequently, three separate six-milliliter cultures were inoculated with the resuspended strain to a starting OD (600 nm) of 0.05. 12C-methanol was added to one culture, 13C-methanol was added to another culture, and 13C-methanol plus the 12C-precursor (final concentration of precursor = 100 μM) was added to the final culture. All cultures were grown at 30C and shaken at 200 rpm. Metabolite extraction and LC-HRMS/MS were performed as previously described.

## Abstract

We present new transit-timing measurements for the white dwarf–cold Jupiter system WD 1856+534, extending the baseline of observations from $311$ epochs to $1498$ epochs. The planet is unlikely to have survived the host star’s red-giant phase at its present location and is likely too small for common envelope evolution to take place. As such, a plausible explanation for the short semimajor axis is that the exoplanet started out on a much larger orbit and then spiraled inward through high-eccentricity tidal migration (HETM). A past study found tentative evidence for orbital growth, which could have been interpreted as a residual effect of HETM, but we find the data are consistent with a constant-period model after adding $18$ new transit measurements. We use the estimated period derivative $\dot{P}=0.04\pm 0.43$ ms yr-1 to place a lower limit on the planetary tidal quality factor of $Q_{p}^{\prime}\gtrsim 3.1\times 10^{6}$ , if the planet has not already achieved spin–orbit synchronization. We also test for the presence of companion planets in the system, which could have excited WD 1856 b onto an eccentric orbit via the Kozai–Lidov process, and ultimately rule out the presence of an additional planet with mass greater than $4.0\,M_{J}$ and period shorter than $1500$ days. We find no evidence for nonzero eccentricity, with an upper limit of $e\lesssim 10^{-2}$ . If the planet reached its current orbit through HETM, the low present-day eccentricity indicates that the migration process has now ceased, and any further orbital evolution, if any, will likely be governed by weak planetary tides.
